title: Ice Age Europeans Were More Connected Than We Thought - Nautilus
gist: A Science Advances study sequencing Gravettian genomes, including the oldest complete genome from southwestern France (Isturitz), shows an east-to-west gene flow around 32,500-31,500 years ago, so eastern and western Ice Age Europeans were less isolated than assumed.

insights.claim: The Gravettian culture lasted roughly 33,000 to 22,000 years ago, and its people were hunter-gatherers who made tanged arrowheads and mammoth-ivory Venus figurines.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie

insights.claim: Gravettians were previously seen as two genetic groups, western Europe and central/eastern Europe.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: The prior consensus the new study challenges.
insights.locator: clustered into two distinct genetic groups

insights.claim: Genomes from Gravettian individuals who lived 30,000 to 22,000 years ago included a woman from Isturitz Cave in southwestern France, giving the oldest complete genome from the region.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Ancient DNA is expanding the resolution of prehistoric population history.
insights.locator: A team of paleogeneticists extracted DNA

insights.claim: The Isturitz woman mostly matched western European lineages but also carried central and eastern European ancestry, and modeling points to an east-to-west gene-flow pulse around 32,500-31,500 years ago.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Population contact across long distances was more common than assumed.
insights.quote: not as genetically isolated as previously assumed
insights.locator: According to the team, most sequences

insights.claim: The findings match genetic data from another Gravettian individual from Ormesson, France, suggesting Isturitz may have been a hub where distant peoples mingled.
